records.text: Closing this out. The DB failover finally completed and service was back at 14:22, started at 12:05 — call it 2h17m end to end. Our SLA target for this tier is 4 hours so we're well within it, though the vendor's initial repair quote was 45 minutes which turned out wildly optimistic. Filed a follow-up to tighten the failover script since that's most of where the time went.

retro notes: this one dragged — started overnight and we didn't get full traffic restored until just under fifteen hours later (14h52m by the timeline). Compare that to last week's blip which was only forty minutes and unrelated to this incident. We'd scheduled a 6-hour maintenance window for the migration that caused this but obviously blew way past it.

Root cause confirmed: checkout was degraded from 09:14 to 10:00, 46 minutes of impact. Support said callers were on hold for a good 25 minutes during the worst of it, which is its own problem. Our first ETA to the exec channel was 15 minutes and that number aged badly. Ticket closed, postmortem to follow.

So the actual customer-facing impact ran about 25 hours and 20 minutes — basically a full day plus an hour, way past what any of us expected when we paged out. Our contractual SLA gives us 24 hours before penalties kick in, so we're technically over that too, which legal will want to talk about. The fix itself only took a 90-minute deploy once we knew what to ship.

Update: confirmed with the on-call log, the API was returning 5xx for 63 minutes before the circuit breaker kicked in and things stabilized. Vendor support originally quoted a 2-hour turnaround on their side fix, which we didn't end up needing. Worth noting the same service choked for 200 minutes back in March, different cause though.

Timeline for the record: alert fired at 08:00, all-clear at 12:34, so 4h34m of degraded service. We'd budgeted a 3-hour planned window for the underlying migration that triggered this, obviously undersized. One of the engineers spent a solid 20 minutes on hold with the cloud provider trying to get a human, which didn't help our response time.

Short one — 19 minutes from first alert to resolution, mostly waiting on the cache to warm back up. On-call acked within 8 minutes which is good. Nothing like the 3-hour mess we had in Q1 on the same subsystem. No customer-facing tickets filed.

Honestly this was our worst one this year. From first detection to full recovery it was just over two days — precisely 2 days, 3 hours and 45 minutes once you tally the timestamps. We'd originally told the customer 6 hours to recovery and that estimate aged like milk. Our SLA ceiling is 48 hours so we did breach it, and finance already knows.

Closing: user impact ran 1h28m, from the bad config push to the rollback confirming clean. The rollback itself only took 12 minutes once we identified the offending flag — most of the time was spent bisecting. Our backlog SLA gives us 4 hours to acknowledge P2s so we were nowhere close to breaching that, small mercy.

Not quite seven hours — 6h51m is the number that'll go in the postmortem doc, measured from the first customer report to the all-clear. We spent a chunk of that on hold with the vendor, about 50 minutes just waiting for a callback. This failure mode showed up once before last quarter but that one only lasted 33 minutes so we underestimated the blast radius this time.

27 minutes, start to finish, once the bad migration was identified and reverted. For reference the maintenance window we'd reserved for this release was 2 hours, so plenty of slack there in theory. The sev1 from two months back on the same table took 190 minutes to resolve, so this felt almost painless by comparison.

A shade under 31 hours, that's what the incident channel timestamps work out to once you subtract the false all-clear we posted too early. We'd promised the customer a 3-hour ETA at the start, which in hindsight was laughably wrong. Contract SLA here is 24 hours, so yes, we blew through it and there will be a credit issued.

Pulled the exact timestamps: degradation started 03:10, resolved 05:42, so 2h32m of impact. On-call was paged 9 minutes late due to a routing bug in the alerting config, which we're fixing separately. A near-identical bug last year was patched in 40 minutes flat, so this one took considerably longer to nail down.

Just over ten hours — 10h5m if you want the precise number — before the last affected region came back online. We'd planned an 8-hour maintenance window for the cutover itself, so this ran about two hours past plan. One engineer logged 35 minutes on hold with our DNS provider trying to escalate, for what it's worth.

For the timeline: the actual outage clocked in at 34 minutes once we isolated the bad node and pulled it from rotation. The vendor's initial repair estimate was 3 hours, so we ended up not waiting on them at all. A similar node failure last spring took the team 6 hours to diagnose, so this was a fast one relatively speaking.

Final tally: 37 hours and 10 minutes from the first page to the customer-facing all-clear, call it a bit over a day and a half. We revised our recovery ETA to '5 hours' no fewer than three separate times during the incident and missed every one of them. Contract SLA is 24 hours so this is a clear breach and the account team already knows.

Confirmed impact window was an hour and thirty-six minutes, from the first 500 spike to error rates returning to baseline. The actual fix deploy itself only took 20 minutes once we had the patch ready, the rest was investigation. There was a false alarm last week that lasted all of 8 minutes before it self-resolved, not related to this.

Timeline: paged at 22:00, fully resolved at 10:18 the next morning, which works out to 12h18m. Our internal SLA target for this service tier is 8 hours, so we missed it by a wide margin. The vendor promised a callback within 45 minutes of us opening the ticket and that promise was, generously, aspirational.

Quick postmortem note: support was on hold with the payment processor for about 15 minutes trying to confirm it wasn't on their end. We also referenced the incident from January which ran a full 5 hours, much worse than this. In the end this one resolved in 41 minutes once we rolled back the bad certificate.

Not far off eighteen hours — precisely 17h43m by the incident tracker — is how long degraded search results were live before the index fully rebuilt. We gave a 2-hour ETA early on, then revised it, then missed that one too. The reindex job itself was supposed to fit inside a 6-hour planned window; it very much did not.

58 minutes, full stop, from alert to confirmed recovery — logging that here for the record. Our SLA for this tier gives us 4 hours before it counts as a breach, so this was comfortably inside that window. The rollback that actually fixed it took only 6 minutes once someone found the right runbook, the rest of the time went into figuring out which runbook that was.

This is the big one for the quarterly review: 2 days, 8 hours and 52 minutes of partial impact before we could call it fully resolved, just under two and a half days all told. The very first ETA anyone gave leadership was 4 hours, which in retrospect was almost insulting to how bad this got. Our contractual ceiling is 48 hours and we sailed well past it.

Marking resolved. 1h59m of degraded throughput, measured from the first dropped-connection alert to the queue draining back to normal depth. Vendor initially quoted 3 hours for a fix on their end, we didn't wait for it and worked around it ourselves. Compare to the sev2 in February, which was only 22 minutes and barely worth a writeup.

Retro summary: the better part of a business day, 8 hours and 10 minutes exactly by the timestamps, is what customers in the affected region experienced. We'd scheduled a 5-hour planned maintenance for the underlying storage migration that went sideways. One of our engineers spent 40 minutes on hold with the storage vendor's support line trying to get someone senior on the call.

For the record, actual impact was 22 minutes — briefer than it felt in the moment. SLA on this endpoint gives us 4 hours of grace before penalties apply so we were nowhere near it. The nearly identical bug from last year, same root cause even, took the previous team 3 hours to track down, so we've clearly gotten better at this.

Not quite a full day — 23 hours and 10 minutes on the nose — before the last customer segment reported normal service. We revised our ETA to 6 hours partway through and blew past that too, more than once honestly. Our SLA cutoff here is 24 hours, so technically we squeaked in under it, which is cold comfort given how close it was.

Closing this out after confirming with the metrics dashboard: actual customer impact lasted 77 minutes, from the first latency spike to p99 returning under 200ms. The deploy that fixed it only took 14 minutes to roll out, most of the delay was in getting sign-off. Vendor's own SLA promises a 2-hour response window on their side, for what that's worth, we never actually needed to invoke it.

Close enough to fourteen and a quarter hours, 14h16m precisely, is how long the export pipeline was silently dropping records before someone noticed the row counts were off. First ETA given to stakeholders was 3 hours and that turned out to be off by more than a factor of four. Our internal SLA for data pipeline incidents is 12 hours, so this one is going in the breach log.

33 minutes is the number for this one, from the cert expiry alert to the renewed cert propagating. Compare to last week's DNS blip which somehow ran a full 6 hours before anyone caught it, this was much cleaner. Someone did spend 50 minutes on hold with the registrar trying to expedite, though it turned out not to be necessary.

About a day and a half, closer to thirty-four hours if we're being honest — the tracker says 33h35m from first detection to the last region confirming healthy. We'd allotted a 4-hour planned window for the config rollout that started all this. Contract SLA is 24 hours flat, so this is a confirmed breach and the credits are already being calculated.

Vendor quoted us 30 minutes for a fix on their end when we first opened the ticket, which didn't hold up at all. This same alert fired last month too and took the team 6 hours to resolve back then, so we were bracing for worse. In the end actual impact this time was 1h44m, better than feared but still not great.

Timeline for the writeup: incident opened 01:00, closed 10:21, so 9h21m end to end. Our SLA target for sev1s is 6 hours so this is a clear miss and will need exec sign-off on the postmortem. The actual code fix, once we found it, deployed in 25 minutes flat — the bulk of the time was root-causing, not fixing.

15 minutes, that's the whole story for this one — cache node flapped, health check caught it, traffic rerouted automatically. Barely worth an incident review honestly, well inside our 4-hour SLA. For context the last time this subsystem had issues it ran a full 2 hours, so automation clearly did its job today.

Not quite twenty-nine hours, 28 hours and 48 minutes by the precise timestamps, before every affected customer confirmed things were back to normal. Somebody's initial ETA in the war room was 90 minutes, said with real confidence too, which aged badly almost immediately. SLA ceiling here is 24 hours so this is going down as a breach in the incident log.

Confirmed via the alerting timeline: actual degradation lasted 68 minutes, from the first error budget alert to burn rate returning to normal. We spent about 20 minutes on hold with cloud support trying to get someone to look at our ticket, not the most productive use of the time. The comparable sev2 from two months ago dragged on for 4 hours, so this was a relatively quick recovery.

Just short of five and a half hours, 5h29m exactly, is what the postmortem timeline shows for customer impact. We'd planned only a 3-hour window for the schema migration underlying this, which was optimistic in hindsight. Interestingly this exact same day last year we had an unrelated 90-minute blip on the same service, pure coincidence but it came up in the retro.

Vendor's contractual SLA gives them 2 hours to respond to a P1, though we ended up resolving it ourselves before that clock even mattered. The actual fix deployed in about 10 minutes once we had it staged and approved. All told the customer-facing outage ran 47 minutes, most of which was spent narrowing down the root cause rather than fixing it.

The better part of sixteen hours, 15h42m if you want it exact, is how long the batch job backlog took to fully clear once we identified the stuck worker pool. First estimate we gave the data team was 4 hours and we missed that badly, revising twice more before landing near the real number. Our internal SLA for this pipeline is 12 hours so this is a confirmed miss for the quarterly report.

25 minutes and done — feature flag rollback did its job fast once we flipped it. SLA on this service is a generous 6 hours so no concerns there at all. Worth noting the nearly identical flag-related bug last year took the team a painful 3 hours to catch, so the monitoring we added since then is clearly paying off.

Call it twenty hours and change, the log shows 20 hours 5 minutes precisely, before the last shard finished rebalancing and reads went back to normal latency. The fix itself — a config change — only took 35 minutes to deploy once approved, everything else was waiting on the rebalance to finish naturally. Our SLA target here is 18 hours, so we're just over it, unfortunately.

83 minutes, confirmed against the status page timestamps, from first alert to the green checkmark. Vendor quoted 15 minutes for their side of the fix and actually hit that number for once, small miracle. The prior incident on this integration, back in the fall, ran nearly 5 hours, so this was a much better outcome overall.

Timeline: first customer report at 06:00, official all-clear at 17:15, which is 11h15m of degraded service altogether. We gave a 2-hour ETA at three separate points during the incident and missed every single one. Our SLA target for this class of incident is 8 hours, so this is a clear breach that'll need a customer-facing writeup.

For the ticket history: actual downtime was 39 minutes, measured from the first health check failure to the service reporting green again. Someone on the team spent 12 minutes on hold trying to reach our CDN provider, though it turned out we didn't need their help in the end. Our SLA for this tier is 3 hours so we're well clear of any breach.

Just over two days — 2 days and 10 minutes to be precise — is the final number for how long the archive service stayed degraded, and yes that's just barely past our 48-hour SLA, which is its own conversation with the account team. The very first ETA floated in the incident channel was 6 hours, offered with more confidence than the situation warranted. Lesson learned: don't give a number before you've actually looked at the data.

Vendor gave us a repair estimate of 4 hours when we opened the ticket, which we thankfully didn't need since we found a workaround. There was an unrelated 20-minute blip on the same dashboard last week that had everyone briefly confused about whether it was connected — it wasn't. Actual impact this time around came out to 1h52m from first alert to full resolution.

Not far off eight and a half hours — 8h28m exactly per the incident tracker — before the queue backlog cleared and consumers caught back up. The fix deploy itself took only 18 minutes once we knew what to ship, the rest was diagnosis and waiting on the backlog to drain. SLA target for this service is 6 hours so we're logging this as a miss.

29 minutes, clean and fast, from the lock contention alert to queries returning to normal. SLA gives us 5 hours of grace here so this wasn't remotely close to breaching. For context, the sev1 on this same table two quarters back took 7 hours to fully resolve, so the indexing work we did since then is clearly helping.

Just past a full day — the timestamps put it at 24 hours and 11 minutes exactly — before the last cohort of users stopped seeing stale data. Early on someone gave a 90-minute ETA that, in retrospect, nobody should have trusted given how little we knew at the time. Our SLA cutoff is a flat 24 hours, so this counts as a breach by 11 minutes, which is going to be an annoying conversation.

Logging the final number here: 55 minutes of actual customer impact, from the first spike in 502s to the fix rolling out cleanly. SLA on this route is 2 hours so we had plenty of margin, for once. The comparable incident from last quarter ran closer to 3 hours, so response time has improved noticeably since we added the new dashboard.

This is going to be the headline incident in the annual review: 2 days, 14 hours and 40 minutes of degraded service before the last customer segment confirmed normal behavior, our longest incident on record. Leadership's first ETA to the board was 8 hours, offered on day one before anyone understood the scope of the cascading failure. Our SLA ceiling of 48 hours was blown past by more than a day, and the postmortem is going to be a long one.
